I have been posting to the WW forum recently, and had theLasombra
point out to me that once a player has obtained a GW, they are
basically free to do whatever they want regarding the remaining VP's
(a fact of which I was not aware).

Does anyone else think this is a strange way for the rest of a game to
be handled?

I did a little bit of a search and found a thread discussing it (how
long 'till you can no longer post a follow up to a another post? I had
to cut and paste).

Messages.Author: evil_poot_cat
Messages.Body:
mud...@hotmail.com (scrote) wrote in message news:<b618d4f6.03052...@posting.google.com>...

> Players must play to win. If a player cannot win, <or
> has already won>, then they must play to maximise their
> VP's.

I disagree here, because pre-win and post-win games are far different.
While the win is still in question, a VP by itself is implicitly a
loss, when compared to a win. Until a table's game win is resolved,
preventing a loss, where someone else scores a win, takes precedence
over maximizing VP (and the associated predator-prey relationship).
I'm not going to guess as to what the remaining players should do
after a game win is scored, but a single VP does take a more prominent
role at that point.

Messages.Author: Ira
Messages.Body:
Currently the tournament rules say that a player must play in a
sportsmanlike manner. For reasons unclear to me, "playing in a
sportsmanlike manner" is defined for V:TES tournaments as "playing to
get a GW; if that's impossible, playing to maximize VPs; if you're
going to get 0 VPs, play however you want."

Everyone who runs tournaments should know that, even though it's not
written in the rules. I propose that it should be stated explicitly
in the tournament rules, but that's besides your point.

I agree that players should be forced to play to maximize VPs. I see
no convincing argument why players should be allowed to give away VPs
after they have the GW. Can anyone state such an argument?

Ira

Messages.Body:
Ira wrote:
> Currently the tournament rules say that a player must play in a
> sportsmanlike manner. For reasons unclear to me, "playing in a
> sportsmanlike manner" is defined for V:TES tournaments as "playing to
> get a GW; if that's impossible, playing to maximize VPs; if you're
> going to get 0 VPs, play however you want."

The reason: The players must play toward the goal stated in the rules.

That is, they can't ignore the goal stated in the rules and act "randomly"
or out of non-game-related spite or what have you. They must play to win.

> I agree that players should be forced to play to maximize VPs. I see
> no convincing argument why players should be allowed to give away VPs
> after they have the GW. Can anyone state such an argument?

After you have won, "play to win" covers pretty much any activity, since
each of your choices leads to a win.

point (and thus the 5-player-table GW), you were reasonably certain in not being able

Come to think of it, this card goes against the very SPIRIT of the play-to-win rule,
doesn't it?

Gambit Accepted
Master
Only usable if you have at least 1 victory point. Lose 1 victory point and put this
card in play. During your untap phase, move 1 pool from your prey's pool to your
pool. If you are ousted, your predator gains an additional victory point. At the end
of the game, if you have not been ousted, you gain an additional victory point.

It may just be me, but I can see A LOT of circumstances where another player at the

What's your point? You're just restating what the rules already say,

_after_ a player has won (but VP's still remain on the table).

> I'm not going to guess as to what the remaining players should do

That's the point. Allowing a winning player to act as they choose

players. _Nothing_ stops the winning player from conceding to the
remaining player (assume it's a friend) to aid their friends chances
of getting into the final.

How can a judge rule against it?

I know it's very remote chance that such a thing will occur, but it
*could*, and *could* so easily fixed so that it *can't*.

made to realise how meaningless this issue is?), I just like talking

Well, when you come down to it, then why aren't players forced to play to
maximize TP's as a tertiary requirement (after GW's and VP's)?

Thus if you're in a 5-player game, and one player has already received 1 or 2
VP's and you're in a no-win situation, then you should be *required* to do your
best to help that player win (whether that means going full-blast forward,
walling up completely, or giving that player all of your resources via the
Succubus Club). Since you can't get any GW's or VP's, you should be forced to
maximize your TP's by trying to ensure that that one player sweeps.

IMO all of that (including dictating further terms to someone who's already
won) seems a little too heavy-handed and really takes away from the concept of
having choices and options. The situation regarding TP's really seems to be a
logical next step from the situation that you (and others) espouse.

unassailable. You may well be able to decide whether you go out before your

I assume this is prey.

>is on 40.

If you cannot improve your standing (TW, followed by VP), you are free
to maintain your current standing in any manner you choose. Assuming
that that manner isn't collusive, or similar.

Additionally, there is a problem with the basic situation you describe,
in that simply having lots of pool is not necessarily indicative of
having an unassailable lead. For instance, your prey may have run out
of cards getting that much pool - or perhaps a badly timed/chosen
Golconda: Inner Peace. You may be playing a strong combat deck. If you
could destroy all his vampires, you could try to oust him. Or, for
instance, you're playing a combat deck with Dramatic Upheavals and so
on. That might put you into a situation where you could oust your
predator, for one VP, instead of obliterating yourself.

Nor does the strategic decision have to, necessarily, be between walling
and hitting. If you have three or four vampires, taking actions with
two and leaving two blockers/bouncers is a possibility. (This can also
feed into the above - a deck with significant bounce potential will be
in a stronger position against a bleed predator than simple pool
standings may look.)

All of these factors can feed in. There are many people who will post
situations which say "Okay, so I can't win..." without actually
explaining *why* it's so difficult for them to not win. Or at least do
better. Simple pool totals don't usually cut it.

It's perfectly possible, in the above example, that you're close to
time. Perhaps it was a four player table - you, LSJ, me, Dave Hammond.

LSJ ousted me. And LSJ is on 1 VP, and 40 pool. You and Dave are on 5
pool and 0 VP. It's towards the end of a long-ish game, possibly. 40
pool... that's a lot of gain, a lot of cards played, probably? Maybe
LSJ doesn't have that great a defence left. You might be able to kill
his minions and get through? Perhaps LSJ and Dave both have no vampires
left...

But let's assume LSJ *does* have some defence. He might not be able to
get through Dave Hammond in time, though. Dave, like you, is thinking
about walling up - and he's probably more precarious. If he holds on,
he might get 0.5 VP for timing out. So he *does* wall up.

LSJ might then make you an offer. You help him get the table win, and
he'll agree to draw with you. You go into Dave and smack him hard,
you'll get a guaranteed 0.5 VP. That's better than your current state
of affairs. You could easily take him up on it. Or, if you're low on
cards, he might let you withdraw after killing Dave. You get 1 VP, he
gets 3 and a TW. Sounds good? Well, it sounds better than how you're
doing if you just rush forward, or even if you just go backwards
randomly.

Or what if LSJ is playing with a Super Arika deck! Or any single
vampire strategy. A laptop, a Pulse of the Canaille, +2 bleed on a
random Inner Circle member, stomping bleeds through. Oh whoops, Archon
Investigation. Sorry, my hand slipped. 3 turns to get a new one out
with 4 transfers a turn, you might have 3 or 4 vampires... he's down
another 11 pool for Arika, you can try and sneak in 10 points of bleed
by then, maybe more... that's a bit different, isn't it?

So these things aren't cut and dried. It might *look* like you have no
hope of a VP from pool totals - but they don't tell you very much.

However, let us assume that LSJ has completely controlled the table.
You have *absolutely no chance* of getting a VP. (The chances of this
are slim, but possible, of course - until you get to the dying seconds.)

You are not colluding with LSJ or Dave Hammond. You have no way of
improving your standing. You may get 0 VP in any manner you choose.
That may include rushing backwards - though some might view that as not
"sporting", even if it might not qualify as unsportsman-like under the
rules, which may be a consideration for you.
